To Consider 1. All indefinite pronouns have a definite connotation when using them. 2. The ones using “Any” mainly work in questions or negative sentences. We use indefinite pronouns to make generalizations about people, places and things.

To consider 1. Indefinite pronouns ending in -body, -one, and -thing refer to people or things without naming them. 2. Pronouns beginning with “any” commonly appear in questions and negative sentences, but they can also appear in positive contexts. 3. Pronouns beginning with “no” already carry a negative meaning. 4. Pronouns ending in -body, -one, and -thing usually take a singular verb: “Everyone is ready.” With all, the verb agrees with the noun after of: “All of the students are ready.”

patches.reason: Teach restrictive and non-restrictive relative clauses with correct punctuation and pronoun choices.

changes.before:
We use relative clauses or relative pronouns to include extra information about someone or something in the sentences.

To consider

1. Most relative pronouns are enclosed between commas. 2. They can also be used as the example with why. 3. How can be used to set clauses related to manners or ways. E.G: I know how he did it!

4. We can also used that to create relative clauses for people and things. Jane, that lives here, is my best friend. The car, that is on the corner, was stolen yesterday.
changes.after:
Use relative clauses to identify someone or something, or to add information.

Identify: no commas; use who, which or that. The student who lives here is my friend.

Add information: use commas and who or which, not that. Jane, who lives here, is my best friend.

Reason / manner: The reason why she left is clear. I know how he did it.
Añade información.

Authored passage/context:
I wasn’t prepared for the culture shock of being an international student For any student, moving away from home can be daunting. But I didn’t expect student life in Scotland to be all that different from my home of the Netherlands. After all, we get the same news and TV shows online. However, when I moved from Amsterdam to study at the University of Stirling, I began to realise that a few small things were catching me off balance. I was suffering a minor cultural shock. In my first year, I quickly found out my English was not as good as I had assumed. Most of my flatmates were born and raised in Scotland, and I constantly found myself having to ask people to repeat themselves. Their Scottish accents didn’t help and I was mispronouncing names and places all the time. I also got confused about small cultural things. Much to my flatmates’ amusement, it took me two Christmases to figure out that mince pies are not actually filled with minced beef. The language barrier meant that public transport was tricky at first. I found the lack of information about bus prices and how and where to get tickets really surprising. It turned a simple 15-minute journey into a daunting task.
